title: Obligation and advice: must, have to, should, ought to
tagline: Rules, warnings and friendly advice — four modal verbs, four different strengths.
why: Reading Part 1 is full of real notices — changing rooms, tournament rules, warning signs — and they live or die on must, mustn't, have to and don't have to. B1 Preliminary also expects you to give advice with should and ought to, and to talk about rules that changed in the past with had to, so this group of modals covers a huge share of the exam's everyday English.

hook.text: Miss Vega: “Players must wear shin pads — no exceptions!” Liam: “Do we have to bring our own ball?” Miss Vega: “No, you don't have to — the club provides one.”
hook.ask: Miss Vega uses three modal verbs in bold to talk about rules. Which one is a strict rule from the organisers, and which one means something isn't necessary?

diagrams.title: Build the sentence

sentences.note: must — a strict rule, the speaker's own authority

diagrams.caption: Mustn't and don't have to look similar but mean opposite things — forbidden vs simply not necessary.

head: Form
Positive
Negative
Question
rows: You mustn't argue with the ref.
You have to bring your kit.
You don't have to bring a ball.

use.point: must vs have to for strong obligation

examples.text: Players must wear shin pads — it's a safety rule.
We have to arrive an hour before kick-off.
examples.note: have to = an outside rule, from the club or competition

examples.text: Every player has to show their student card at the gate.
examples.note: an external rule again, not the speaker's opinion

use.point: mustn't vs don't have to / needn't

examples.text: You don't have to bring your own ball — the club provides one.
examples.note: don't have to = not necessary, your choice

examples.text: You needn't worry about the weather; the final is indoors.
examples.note: needn't = the same idea as don't have to, more formal

use.point: should, ought to and had better for advice

examples.text: You should warm up properly before the match.
examples.note: should = friendly advice, not a rule

examples.text: The team ought to practise penalties this week.
examples.note: ought to = advice, a little more formal than should

examples.text: You'd better hurry — the match starts in five minutes!
examples.note: had better = strong advice, almost a warning

use.point: had to / didn't have to in the past, and be allowed to

examples.text: Last year, players had to bring their own shin pads.
examples.note: had to = the past of must/have to for obligation

examples.text: Substitutes are allowed to warm up on the side of the pitch.
examples.note: be allowed to = permission, another useful modal idea

watch_out.wrong: You mustn't bring your own ball if you don't want to.
watch_out.right: You don't have to bring your own ball.
watch_out.why: Mustn't means forbidden; for something that's simply not necessary, use don't have to or needn't.

watch_out.wrong: We must arrive early, the club says it's a rule.
watch_out.right: We have to arrive early — it's the club's rule.
watch_out.why: For someone else's rule, have to sounds more natural than must, which suggests the speaker's own authority.

watch_out.wrong: You should wear shin pads, it's the law of the tournament.
watch_out.right: You must wear shin pads — it's a rule of the tournament.
watch_out.why: A strict, official rule needs must or have to, not should, which is only advice.

watch_out.wrong: Last year, players must bring their own kit.
watch_out.right: Last year, players had to bring their own kit.
watch_out.why: Must has no past form — use had to for past obligation.

watch_out.wrong: You don't must argue with the referee.
watch_out.why: The negative of must is mustn't, not don't must.

watch_out.wrong: Do you must pay for the tickets?
watch_out.right: Do you have to pay for the tickets?
watch_out.why: Must has no question form with do — use have to for questions about obligation.

l1.wrong: You have to wear shin pads, it's my advice.
l1.why: Debes as friendly advice from a person is should, not the stronger have to.

l1.es: No tienes que traer el balón.
l1.right: You don't have to bring the ball.
l1.why: Spanish no tienes que means it isn't necessary — that's don't have to, not the prohibition mustn't.

l1.es: No debes discutir con el árbitro.
l1.wrong: You don't have to argue with the referee.
l1.why: No debes here means it is forbidden — that's mustn't, a stronger idea than don't have to.

l1.es: Tuvimos que llegar temprano el año pasado.
l1.wrong: We must arrive early last year.
l1.right: We had to arrive early last year.
l1.why: Must has no past tense; the past of obligation is always had to.

remember.trick: MUST is you; HAVE TO is the rule outside you!
remember.tip: Mustn't = forbidden. Don't have to = not necessary. Never mix the two up.

dialogue.title: Rules for the final
dialogue.context: Before the school football final, Miss Vega explains the rules to Liam, Mateo, Sofia and Nadia.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Listen up — players must wear shin pads. No exceptions.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Do we have to bring our own ball?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: No, you don't have to — the club provides one.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Do we have to pay for the tickets too?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: You needn't worry about that — it's free for students.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Remember, players mustn't argue with the referee.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: And you'd better warm up properly — it's really hot today!

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Good advice. You should also drink plenty of water.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Last year we had to bring our own kit — is that still true?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: No, this year the school allows you to borrow one if you need it.

items.sentence: The referee says: players ___ wear shin pads.
items.why: a strict rule, the speaker's own authority

items.sentence: We ___ arrive an hour before kick-off — it's the club's rule.
items.why: someone else's rule, not the speaker's own

items.sentence: You ___ bring your own ball — the club provides one.
You ___ warm up properly before the match.
items.why: friendly advice, not a strict rule

items.sentence: Last year, players ___ bring their own kit.
___ you have to pay for the tickets?
You ___ worry about the weather — the final is indoors.
items.why: not necessary, more formal than don't have to

practice.instructions: Put the words in order. Tap them one by one.

items.answer: We have to arrive an hour before kick-off.
You don't have to bring your own ball.
Players mustn't argue with the referee.
You should warm up before the match.
Players had to bring their own kit last year.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it means the same as the first, using the word given.

items.first: It's a safety rule — shin pads are compulsory for players.
The club's rule says we need to arrive an hour early.
It isn't necessary to bring your own ball.
Arguing with the referee is forbidden.
My advice is to warm up before the match.

can_do: I can talk about strong obligation with must and have to, and know when to use each one.
I can tell the difference between mustn't (forbidden) and don't have to (not necessary).
I can give advice with should, ought to and had better, and talk about past obligation with had to.
summary: Must = the speaker's own authority; have to = a rule that comes from somewhere else.
Mustn't = forbidden; don't have to / needn't = not necessary, your choice.
Should, ought to and had better give advice — they aren't strict rules.
Must has no past form: use had to for obligation in the past.
Be allowed to talks about permission, a different idea from obligation.
